Tammy Taylor

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Fabulous franchise or polished Ponzi scheme? The claws are out in a multimillion Rand spat.

Unique Selling Point:
Four case studies (representative of a group of 20) who invested millions into their Tammy Taylor nail salons have become disenchanted, disenfranchised and almost destitute following disagreements with franchise holders Peet & Melany Viljoen. They accuse the couple of setting them up to fail, offering no support, and burdening them with hidden costs that prevent them from ever making a profit. When they sound the alarm, the Viljoens urge them to sell their business at a fraction of their investment, and then resell the salon to another buyer.


Summary:
The license fee is R345 000. Peet claims to have sold 300 licenses, but there are only 20 Tammy Taylor salons in South Africa. Some people have paid almost R1 m for a salon, but were never given the keys.
All franchisees have to use shoplifters recommended by Peet, who charge 3 times the going rate.
All stock has to be ordered from the Viljoens, who increase the price by 100% willy nilly and invoice for exchange rate fluctuations long after delivery.
Monthly royalties are charged at 7% of turnover, but the Viljoens insist that is before the deduction of VAT. They then charge VAT on top of the 7% royalty. According to the franchisees the Viljoens have not paid that VAT to SARS.


Further information:
Peet and Melany Viljoen - the Barbie and Ken of Pretoria East are no strangers to controversy. Once a celebrity lawyer, Viljoen’s career as an attorney came to an end in September 2011 when two Pretoria High Court judges concurred that it would be in the best interest of the law profession and the public for him to be barred from practicing. He is now the CEO of Tammy Taylor South Africa, and also acts a "law broker", advising clients on the best legal team. He has now reinvented himself a philanthropist, distributing masks, sanitiser and water to the poor and then writing about it in local Caxton papers, calling himself "The James Bond of Philanthropy."

Extra Budget Items:
Possible extra half day for cameraman and Derek if Tammy Taylor agrees to an interview.

Script:


TAMMY TAYLOR

V/O: It’s the cutting edge of beauty, but according to some unhappy franchisees Tammy Taylor Nails has begun to lose lustre.

Jennelle: If I had to turn back the hands of time, I would have definitely not bought into this franchise.

Taryn: It’s derailed my entire life.

Ntombi: I feel like I’m about to lose everything that I’ve invested.

Daniella: It was the worst experience of my life.

Derek link: Tammy Taylor Nails is billed as the lap of luxury, complete with French champagne and superior products. From here it all looks peachy but is this a fantastic franchise opportunity?

V/O: The real Tammy Taylor is an American entrepreneur. Tammy Taylor Nails South Africa is owned by Mel Viljoen who started a franchise business with husband Peet Viljoen.

Sfx: Hi, I’m Peet Viljoen.

V/O: Now Tammy Taylor’s CEO, Peet is a disgraced lawyer. In 2011 he was struck off the Roll by the Pretoria High Court. A few years later he opened what he called “South Africa’s first law brokerage.”

Peet: I’m best equipped, after 18 years of practicing as a lawyer, to appoint the right legal team to a specific problem.

Derek: Who is the driving force at Tammy Taylor?

Taryn: Peet Viljoen is absolutely the driving force.

V/O: After paying R345 000 for the franchise license, Taryn Dunnett co-signed a lease with Tammy Taylor for the Dainfern Square store in Sandton.

Derek: So how much have you invested in total?

Taryn: From inception I would say about R2.5 million, and then another million in the 7 months that I was running. The bulk of it was my pension, after leaving the bank after 17 years.

V/O: Despite being in a premium location Taryn claims she was barely breaking even. Every month, she struggled to pay her rent and the 7% royalty fee.

Taryn: Then in December we got an email saying that stock prices are increasing by 50% and obviously that threw us even more. But with the stock prices I couldn’t afford to buy more stock, I couldn’t afford royalties. My rent I would literally pay as I got money in on a daily basis.

Derek: How much did you owe Tammy Taylor in royalties?

Taryn: About 33K.

V/O: According to the Franchise Agreement, Tammy Taylor is entitled to cancel the contract if a franchisee fails to pay royalties or rent on time. And Taryn was in arrears, so on the 27th of February a cancellation letter was sent to her. Two days later she found herself locked out of her own store.

Derek: Was that legal in your opinion?

Taryn: No. not in my opinion and not in the Court’s opinion either.

V/O: She launched an urgent interdict and on the 6th March the Pretoria High Court granted possession of the store to Taryn. But when she returned to the premises that afternoon with the Sheriff and a locksmith, but the new owner refused to let her in.

Sfx: What are they doing? It’s a court order.”

Taryn: It was getting to a point where I felt there could be imminent violence. The people who came as her security had weapons.

V/O: When we approached Tammy Taylor Nails for answers, the CEO Peet Viljoen nominated his wife Mel to do the interview.

Derek link: This is the Tammy Taylor Head Office in Pretoria. We had an interview confirmed with Mel Viljoen for 11’clock, but after we sent them our questions, they decided to cancel the interview and give written answers instead.

V/O: But the next day Mel changed her mind and agreed to appear on camera. Unfortunately I was in a furnace in Mpumalanga at the time, so our Producer took on the interview.

Kate: The High Court issued an Order to return possession of the store to Taryn. Why was that ignored?

Mel: That’s a great question for Ruann to answer as well, because there is a good reason for it.

V/O: Mel bounced the question to her lawyer, Ruann Kruger.

Ruan: Because we are of the opinion that the Judge made a mistake. It’s appealable and any appeal suspends any order that was made.

V/O: The new owner got an urgent court order suspending Taryn’s order until the Appeal is resolved.

Ruan: The landlord actually closed the locks, they weren’t paid, and obviously handed back the keys back to us because we were the head lease. It’s in our name.

Taryn: They started trading the day they kicked me out of my store with my staff, with my computer, my business cellphone, my property – everything in that store.

V/O: We asked Mel about the increased stock prices.

Mel: The increase came from the Rand Dollar exchange, but we absorbed the increase for most of the franchisees. To the franchisees that did not contribute equally to the brand, only they got a price increase for stock.

Derek link: This is the Dainfern Square store where the claws came out. Tammy Taylor in the meantime, have sold the store lock, stock and chandelier to someone else.

Taryn: I’ve literally lost everything.

V/O: In 2018 Daniella Angelides opened the Groenkloof store in Pretoria.

Daniella: In total it cost me R1.3 million to open my store. There wasn’t one month I walked out with money in my pocket.

V/O: In November last year she decided to sell.

Daniela: I had agreed I would go down to 850 000. I got a phone call from Mel and she said would I go down to 500 000?

V/O: Daniella agreed and received an email from Tammy Taylor Nails confirming they had sold her store for R500 000.

Daniela: And the deal was R350 000 to be paid in December and I have an additional 150 000 to be paid in March this year. And that, I’m still waiting for.

V/O: The buyer of the Groenkloof store was Pinky Nxumalo.

Daniela: The first time I met Pinky was the day of takeover. She had never met Mel or Peet. She hadn’t even signed a franchise agreement. It then came to my attention that she had already paid Peet 790 000 with an additional 150 000 to be paid. Peet had told me that he could only get us R500 000 for the salon. And when I brought this to their attention, they basically told me to get out. It’s not my salon anymore.

V/O: The Angelides have since issued summons to Tammy Taylor Nails for the outstanding R150 000.

Kate: Why didn’t you pay the remaining 150?

Mel: We need to pause and we need to talk to Ruan quickly.

Ruan: I know there’s an amount that was paid to Daniella and I know there’s an amount outstanding. I don’t know who’s owing who? There’s a dispute about what Pinky paid and what Daniella received.

Mel: She didn't buy from us. She buyed directly from the previous owner.

Kate: But Pinky didn't pay her. You paid her.

Mel: So Pinky paid us and we pay Daniela.

Kate: And how much did she pay you? How much did you sell the salon to Pinky for?

Mel: I feel like um, we’ve answered that question already.

V/O: Pinky paid a total of R827 000 in 4 separate payments to Tammy Taylor Nails, and another company owned by Mel Viljoen, American Branding. But realizing how much more was needed to make the salon viable, she never signed the franchise agreement and wants her money back.

Mel: She just locked the doors. As a brand, we have a have footprint and we have to make sure that every woman out there has Tammy Taylor nails on them.

V/O: The Groenkloof store is now owned by Cherese Kruger, the wife of the Tammy Taylor’s lawyer, Ruann Kruger.

Derek: So how much did you pay for the store?

Cherise: I only paid R300 000 for the franchise fee.

Derek link: Tammy Taylor Nails SA claim to have sold over 300 licenses, and yet only know of 38 stores. But now, the owner of one of the most profitable and prestigious stores has decided to add her voice to the chorus of disapproval.

Jennelle: I think they are there just to make money on the license fees, because they are not looking after their franchises.

V/O: Jennelle Joshi says when she disputed the VAT being charged on royalties, Tammy Taylor Nails withheld stock to her busy salon. All franchisees may only use Tammy Taylor products. She brought an urgent application to release the stock - but lost the case. Tammy Taylor say her royalties were in arrears and they were entitled to stop supplying her.

Jennelle: So we have lodged an appeal to appeal the decision.
So I’ve been running around ordering stock from the franchisees that have closed down.

V/O: But while the litigation was in progress, Tammy Taylor accused Jannelle of using other products.

Jennelle: They take a sample of your liquid. They say they’ve taken it to a lab to test it, but they can’t provide you with a lab report to show you that it’s not Tammy Taylor, but it was Tammy Taylor liquid.

Kate: She denies using different products?

Mel: We’ve got pictures.

V/O: These are photocopies of those pictures. Tammy Taylor cancelled her franchise agreement. She is now fighting this in court to try and protect her R1.8 million investment.

Jennelle: In that same week there was a buyer in my salon. This guy came in and said he was sent by Head Office because he is going to purchase the salon. But my salon is not for sale.

Mel: The Marc de-franchised legally, legitimately. She received the letter unless she claims that her email address was wrong as well.

V/O: In March last year the San Ridge Mall salon in Midrand had a champagne launch. The owner, Ntombi Khambule, says it represents a R3.2 million investment.

Derek: Has the investment paid off?

Ntombi: Not at all, because I’m actually sitting in a position where it’s either I sell or just close doors right now.

V/O: Her financial trouble started when Ntombi bought a second license for Polo Fields shopping centre which is still under construction.

Ntombi: I paid the franchise fee amount, but we did not sign an agreement.

Derek: You just paid it over?

Ntombi: Yes.

V/O: When she decided not to go ahead with the Polo Fields store, Head Office refused to refund the license fee. They also refused to offset the amount against stock and royalties, insisting that she pay in full.

Ntombi: So I then approached my lawyers to say this is the problem I’m having. Can we actually handle this? But from then they told me I will not receive any stock from them if I’m litigating with them.

Mel: She was a great partner, but when she started taking the law into her own hands, started asking us to give her a refund and she’s not going to pay royalties…

Ntombi: I think they should treat franchisees with a little bit more empathy, and not see them as cash cows.

V/O: Peet Viljoen gave us the names of 10 salons to canvas their opinion. They all said they were happy with the franchisor. 5 have only been open a few weeks. Ntombi Mason has owned the Moreleta Park salon for 3 years.

Ntombi: It’s something I’ve always wanted to do and I can never say it’s anything other than great.

Mel: We’re going to keep selling franchises, we’re going to keep taking over stores if people don’t pay their fees. That is just the way business is. It’s not personal, and I feel people should not take it personal.

She brought an urgent application to release the stock - but lost the case. Tammy Taylor say her royalties were in arrears and they were entitled to stop supplying her. Jennelle: So we have lodged an appeal to appeal the decision. So I’ve been running around ordering stock from the franchisees that have closed down. V/O: But while the litigation was in progress, Tammy Taylor accused Jannelle of using other products. Jennelle: They take a sample of your liquid. They say they’ve taken it to a lab to test it, but they can’t provide you with a lab report to show you that it’s not Tammy Taylor, but it was Tammy Taylor liquid. Kate: She denies using different products? Mel: We’ve got pictures. V/O: These are photocopies of those pictures. Tammy Taylor cancelled her franchise agreement. She is now fighting this in court to try and protect her R1.8 million investment. Jennelle: In that same week there was a buyer in my salon. This guy came in and said he was sent by Head Office because he is going to purchase the salon. But my salon is not for sale. Mel: The Marc de-franchised legally, legitimately. She received the letter unless she claims that her email address was wrong as well. V/O: In March last year the San Ridge Mall salon in Midrand had a champagne launch. The owner, Ntombi Khambule, says it represents a R3.2 million investment. Derek: Has the investment paid off? Ntombi: Not at all, because I’m actually sitting in a position where it’s either I sell or just close doors right now. V/O: Her financial trouble started when Ntombi bought a second license for Polo Fields shopping centre which is still under construction. Ntombi: I paid the franchise fee amount, but we did not sign an agreement. Derek: You just paid it over? Ntombi: Yes. V/O: When she decided not to go ahead with the Polo Fields store, Head Office refused to refund the license fee. They also refused to offset the amount against stock and royalties, insisting that she pay in full. Ntombi: So I then approached my lawyers to say this is the problem I’m having. Can we actually handle this? But from then they told me I will not receive any stock from them if I’m litigating with them. Mel: She was a great partner, but when she started taking the law into her own hands, started asking us to give her a refund and she’s not going to pay royalties… Ntombi: I think they should treat franchisees with a little bit more empathy, and not see them as cash cows. V/O: Peet Viljoen gave us the names of 10 salons to canvas their opinion. They all said they were happy with the franchisor. 5 have only been open a few weeks. Ntombi Mason has owned the Moreleta Park salon for 3 years. Ntombi: It’s something I’ve always wanted to do and I can never say it’s anything other than great. Mel: We’re going to keep selling franchises, we’re going to keep taking over stores if people don’t pay their fees. That is just the way business is. It’s not personal, and I feel people should not take it personal. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Fabulous franchise or polished Ponzi scheme? The claws are out in a multimillion Rand spat.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Four case studies (representative of a group of 20) who invested millions into their Tammy Taylor nail salons have become disenchanted, disenfranchised and almost destitute following disagreements with franchise holders Peet & Melany Viljoen. They accuse the couple of setting them up to fail, offering no support, and burdening them with hidden costs that prevent them from ever making a profit. When they sound the alarm, the Viljoens urge them to sell their business at a fraction of their investment, and then resell the salon to another buyer.
metadata.Summary: The license fee is R345 000. Peet claims to have sold 300 licenses, but there are only 20 Tammy Taylor salons in South Africa. Some people have paid almost R1 m for a salon, but were never given the keys. All franchisees have to use shoplifters recommended by Peet, who charge 3 times the going rate. All stock has to be ordered from the Viljoens, who increase the price by 100% willy nilly and invoice for exchange rate fluctuations long after delivery. Monthly royalties are charged at 7% of turnover, but the Viljoens insist that is before the deduction of VAT. They then charge VAT on top of the 7% royalty. According to the franchisees the Viljoens have not paid that VAT to SARS.
metadata.Further information: Peet and Melany Viljoen - the Barbie and Ken of Pretoria East are no strangers to controversy. Once a celebrity lawyer, Viljoen’s career as an attorney came to an end in September 2011 when two Pretoria High Court judges concurred that it would be in the best interest of the law profession and the public for him to be barred from practicing. He is now the CEO of Tammy Taylor South Africa, and also acts a "law broker", advising clients on the best legal team. He has now reinvented himself a philanthropist, distributing masks, sanitiser and water to the poor and then writing about it in local Caxton papers, calling himself "The James Bond of Philanthropy."
